title: Temporal Correlations and Optimal Feedback Control of an Active Information Engine
abstract: How much does a feedback controller need to know about the fluctuations it exploits? We address this question using a macroscopic information engine driven by self-propelled bristle-robots. Experimentally measured occupancy time series show that temporal correlations strongly affect vacancy detection. At short measurement intervals, mean first-passage times exceed independent-measurement predictions by more than an order of magnitude. A first-order Markov approximation captures much of this effect. It does not reproduce the full first-passage distribution, revealing higher-order temporal memory. Nevertheless, Markov-selected protocols come within 0.15\% of the maximum experimental power. Neglecting correlations causes power losses of several percent and favors larger compression distances. Introducing a sensing cost shifts the optimal strategy toward sparse sensing. The independent model cannot predict this shift, whereas the Markov model captures it. Cross-validation on separate time segments confirms the near-optimal performance of Markov-selected protocols. These findings demonstrate that near-optimal feedback control in correlated nonequilibrium systems can require a simpler statistical description than predicting their full temporal dynamics.
summary: This work analyzes an active information engine powered by self-propelled robots, focusing on how temporal correlations in the measurement signal affect work extraction. The authors demonstrate that while the true dynamics may have complex memory, using a simple first-order Markov model is sufficient to design protocols that achieve near-optimal power output. This highlights that for optimal control, a simplified statistical description can be highly effective.
main_problem: The paper investigates how much knowledge of temporal correlations in a fluctuating environment is necessary to achieve near-optimal feedback control for extracting work from an active information engine.
main_result: Near-optimal control can be achieved using a simple first-order Markov description, even though the full dynamics exhibit higher-order memory, demonstrating that simplicity can suffice for near-optimal performance.
method: The authors compare the performance (power output) of feedback protocols derived from three statistical models: independent measurements, first-order Markov approximations, and the full experimental data.
model_or_system: The system is a macroscopic information engine driven by self-propelled bristle-robots, which measures the occupancy of a region ($\Delta x$) via a binary signal $A(t)$. The engine advances a piston upon detecting an empty region.

main_assumptions: The analysis compares predictions from the independent model and the first-order Markov approximation against empirical measurements, noting that the Markov model is sufficient for near-optimal control.
figures_summary: Figures compare experimental occupancy signals and first-passage time statistics against predictions from independent and Markov models, showing close agreement near optimal operating points.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical setup and observables, compares the predictive power of independent vs. Markov models for waiting times, analyzes power loss due to correlation neglect, and concludes by validating the Markov model's near-optimality via cross-validation.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete example of how non-equilibrium statistical mechanics governs energy extraction in active matter, showing that complex dynamics can be effectively modeled by simpler Markovian descriptions for practical optimization.

Figure 3(b) shows the experimental power landscape as a function of the normalized compression distance δx = ∆x/Lx and measurement interval τm, at Φ = 0.053. Increasing the compression distance increases the work extracted per cycle, but reduces the probability of de- tecting an empty region, leading to longer waiting times. This competition produces a power maximum at an in- termediate compression distance. Temporal correlations shift its location. Frequent measurements probe strongly correlated configurations, so reducing τm does not pro- portionally reduce the waiting time for a vacancy.
